clue.text: Composer of Planets air/variations

indicators.note: musical variations rework a theme, so the letters of the two words before are reworked too

explanation.surface: A tune from Holst's suite The Planets, played with variations, credited to some composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variations' rearranges PLANETS and AIR. Palestrina was a sixteenth-century Italian composer of church music.
explanation.definitionFit: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina was a Renaissance Italian composer of sacred music.

clue.text: Good fellow severely knocked about at ice hockey

definitions.text: severely knocked about at ice hockey

explanation.surface: A decent man takes a beating on the rink.
explanation.walkthrough: Robin Goodfellow is another name for the mischievous sprite of A Midsummer Night's Dream; the disc in ice hockey is hit hard all game.
explanation.definitionFit: Robin Goodfellow is the folk sprite of that name, and the rubber disc struck by sticks in ice hockey bears it too.

clue.text: Siren with secret knowledge gets floral tribute

parts.note: lore is traditional knowledge handed down among initiates
a lei is a Hawaiian garland of flowers given in welcome

explanation.surface: A seductress with hidden wisdom is presented with flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lorelei is the Rhine maiden of legend whose singing lured boatmen to their deaths, a river siren.

clue.text: Dreiser work retraces Iris, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of the two words before might be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: A Theodore Dreiser novel retells the life of a woman called Iris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges RETRACES and IRIS. Sister Carrie (1900) was Theodore Dreiser's first novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Sister Carrie is the 1900 novel by the American writer Theodore Dreiser.

clue.text: Severe criticism of Pig by Lamb

explanation.surface: A harsh review of a piece on pork by the essayist Charles Lamb.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Lamb wrote the essay 'A Dissertation upon Roast Pig'; the treatment that pig got is the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A harsh dressing-down is called this, and it is also the cooking Lamb's famous pig essay describes.

clue.text: Hodge finally gets its point in play

definitions.text: Hodge finally gets its point in play

parts.words: Hodge finally gets its point in play
parts.note: in the Tudor comedy Gammer Gurton's ___, the lost sewing tool is at last found when it pricks the servant Hodge in his breeches

explanation.surface: A rustic finally sees the point in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: Gammer Gurton's Needle is an early English comedy; the lost needle turns up in Hodge's breeches when he sits on it.
explanation.definitionFit: The sewing implement lost in Gammer Gurton's comedy is found when its sharp point jabs Hodge.

clue.text: First chap to be a mother

parts.note: a dam is the mother of an animal, especially livestock

explanation.surface: The first man is destined to become a mother.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis he is the first man created, so the first chap of all.

clue.text: Word guide provided by ray refracted on this speech

indicators.note: refracted light is bent and broken up, so the letters of the word guide are broken up, with ray's set aside

parts.note: a dictionary is a guide to words

explanation.surface: A dictionary explains light rays bending, as heard in a lecture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refracted' signals that DICTIONARY is a jumble of the answer plus RAY: take out R, A, Y and the rest is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Diction is a manner of enunciation, the way words are spoken.

clue.text: Madrigalist curiously met no opera composer

indicators.note: curiously signals the letters of met no are arranged in an odd way

parts.note: Giuseppe Verdi composed Aida, Rigoletto and La traviata

explanation.surface: A madrigal writer strangely never encountered an opera composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curiously' rearranges MET NO into MONTE. Monteverdi wrote books of madrigals and early operas.
explanation.definitionFit: Claudio Monteverdi published nine books of madrigals, the part-song form of the Italian Renaissance.

clue.text: "She stole along, she nothing spoke, / The sighs she heaved were soft and low"

definitions.text: "She stole along, she nothing spoke, / The sighs she heaved were soft and low"

parts.words: She stole along, she nothing spoke, / The sighs she heaved were soft and low
parts.note: lines from Coleridge's unfinished Gothic poem, describing its heroine creeping through the castle at night

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from Coleridge's poem of 1816, named after its heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: The quoted lines describe the heroine of Coleridge's Gothic poem, who gives it its title.

clue.text: Obey metric rules in examination

explanation.surface: Following the rules of verse in a test.
explanation.definitionFit: Verse that fits its metre is said to do this, and a close inspection, as in a medical image, is the other sense.

clue.text: Kidnap victim is both king and prime minister

parts.note: David was the biblical king of Israel (and the name of Scottish kings)
Arthur Balfour was British prime minister 1902-05

explanation.surface: Someone abducted turns out to be both a monarch and a premier.
explanation.walkthrough: Stevenson's Kidnapped has a hero, abducted onto a ship by his uncle, whose name combines a king and a prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: The hero of Stevenson's Kidnapped is seized and shipped off by his scheming uncle.

clue.text: Very rare treatment of Sharpe steak

definitions.text: Very rare treatment of Sharpe steak

parts.words: Very rare treatment of Sharpe steak
parts.note: a steak barely seared is cooked this way, and Tom Sharpe's comic novel adds the word to the cut called porterhouse

explanation.surface: How a chef serves a steak almost raw.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Sharpe's Cambridge satire is Porterhouse Blue; porterhouse is also a cut of steak, and a steak served almost raw is ordered blue.
explanation.definitionFit: A steak seared only on the outside is served this way, and Sharpe's Porterhouse novel ends with the word.

clue.text: "(He) became very — over his second glass of port felix holt"

definitions.text: "(He) became very — over his second glass of port felix holt"

parts.words: (He) became very — over his second glass of port felix holt
parts.note: a sentence from George Eliot's novel Felix Holt with one word missing, a word for chatty

explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap in the quotation from George Eliot's Felix Holt, the Radical.
explanation.definitionFit: Port loosens the tongue: the missing word means chatty or loquacious.

clue.text: Carson McCullers told us it would be wonderful multiplied by itself

definitions.text: Carson McCullers told us it would be wonderful multiplied by itself

parts.words: Carson McCullers told us it would be wonderful multiplied by itself
parts.note: McCullers's 1957 play is titled The ___ of Wonderful, and the number which multiplied by itself gives a value has this mathematical name

explanation.surface: A novelist promises that doubling one's joy would be marvellous.
explanation.walkthrough: Carson McCullers's play is The Square Root of Wonderful; a square root multiplied by itself gives the original number.
explanation.definitionFit: A number that multiplied by itself makes a given value is that value's square root, as in McCullers's play title.

clue.text: French who number a hundred at university, number ten in Palliser book

parts.note: qui is French for who
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
X is the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.surface: A tally of French people, a hundred at college, ten in a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Palliser's Victorian-pastiche novel The Quincunx (1989) takes its title from the five-point pattern.
explanation.definitionFit: The Quincunx is Charles Palliser's long 1989 mystery novel set in nineteenth-century England.

clue.text: She spent Happy Days with a sandcastle

definitions.text: She spent Happy Days with a sandcastle

parts.words: She spent Happy Days with a sandcastle
parts.note: in Beckett's play Happy Days the heroine is buried up to her waist, then her neck, in a mound of sand

explanation.surface: A girl enjoyed a seaside holiday building sandcastles.
explanation.walkthrough: The heroine of Beckett's Happy Days spends the play buried in a mound of earth, here wittily called a sandcastle.
explanation.definitionFit: Beckett's heroine of Happy Days is buried in a heap of sand throughout the play.

clue.text: Ten Morse mysteries in short story with a moral

indicators.note: a mystery jumbles the facts, so these letters are jumbled too

explanation.surface: Ten Inspector Morse mysteries collected as moral tales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mysteries' rearranges TEN MORSE; Morse is Colin Dexter's Oxford detective.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief homily or little sermon, the kind of short piece that ends on a lesson.

clue.text: Northern Olympus over the rainbow

explanation.surface: Somewhere over the rainbow lies the home of the northern gods.
explanation.walkthrough: In Norse myth the gods' home is reached by Bifrost, the rainbow bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Asgard is the home of the Norse gods, a northern counterpart to Olympus, reached across the rainbow bridge Bifrost.

clue.text: Sort of writing that will haunt the reader?

definitions.text: Sort of writing that will haunt the reader?

parts.words: Sort of writing that will haunt the reader?
parts.note: writing done anonymously for someone else is named after a spectre, so whimsically it might haunt the reader

explanation.surface: A creepy kind of book that stays with you.
explanation.walkthrough: A book written for another to sign is produced by a ghost writer; the clue plays on spectres haunting.
explanation.definitionFit: A book written by a hired writer under someone else's name is said to have been this.

clue.text: Essential directors of electronic instrument

parts.note: key means essential, as in a key point
a board is a company's group of directors

explanation.surface: The chief managers of an electronics firm.
explanation.definitionFit: An electronic keyed instrument, such as a synthesiser, is called this.

clue.text: "O coward conscience, how dost thou — me?" (Richard III)

definitions.text: "O coward conscience, how dost thou — me?" (Richard III)

parts.words: O coward conscience, how dost thou — me?
parts.note: Richard's line on waking from his nightmare before Bosworth, with the verb meaning torment or trouble missing

explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap in Richard's speech in Act 5 of Shakespeare's Richard III.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means to torment or distress, which is what Richard's conscience does.

clue.text: Last resort of Hadrian?

parts.note: the emperor built his great country villa in the hill town east of Rome and retired there late in life

explanation.surface: What the emperor turned to when all else failed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last resort' means a final retreat: Hadrian's Villa is at a hill town near Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: Hadrian built his villa at this town east of Rome, his final retreat, here wittily his last resort.

clue.text: Strange but essential characteristic of all that foreign stuff

definitions.text: Strange but essential characteristic of all that foreign stuff

parts.words: Strange but essential characteristic of all that foreign stuff
parts.note: the quality of being strange and foreign; read cryptically as the word for strange plus a suffix for a doctrine

explanation.surface: The odd but defining trait of everything from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the word for strange plus -ISM, the quality that defines whatever comes from foreign parts.
explanation.definitionFit: The quality of being foreign or unusual, or a taste for the alien and strange.

clue.text: Long sentence in biography

explanation.surface: A lengthy prison term in a book about someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A prison term with no fixed end is so called, and a written account of a person's history is another sense.

clue.text: Philosopher not quite "in the zone"

indicators.note: not quite suggests the letters of zone are not quite in their right order

explanation.surface: A thinker is almost in a state of total focus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' rearranges ZONE. Zeno of Elea posed the paradoxes of motion; Zeno of Citium founded Stoicism.
explanation.definitionFit: Zeno of Elea, famous for his paradoxes of motion, was a Greek thinker.

clue.text: A mate of Richard Hughes

parts.note: in Richard Hughes's novel A High Wind in Jamaica, the pirate ship's mate bears this name

explanation.surface: A friend of a Welsh novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mate' looks like friend; it is a ship's officer in A High Wind in Jamaica.
explanation.definitionFit: The pirate captain Jonsen's mate in A High Wind in Jamaica is named Otto.

clue.text: Climb tree to find Durrell's diplomat

parts.note: to mount is to climb
the olive is a Mediterranean tree

explanation.surface: Scale a tree to track down a diplomat from a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Mountolive is the British ambassador in Lawrence Durrell's Alexandria Quartet, and titles its third volume.
explanation.definitionFit: David Mountolive is the British envoy in Egypt in Durrell's Alexandria Quartet.

clue.text: Edna O'Brien found she could make a theme of it, given time

definitions.text: Edna O'Brien found she could make a theme of it, given time

parts.words: Edna O'Brien found she could make a theme of it, given time
parts.note: O'Brien's 1992 novel is Time and ___, so with time added this word makes her subject

explanation.surface: An Irish novelist discovered a subject once she had the hours.
explanation.walkthrough: Edna O'Brien's novel is Time and Tide; 'given time' means paired with the word time.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea's rise and fall is meant, the second word of O'Brien's novel title after time.

clue.text: Jacopo Robusti, little dyer of Venice

explanation.surface: A Venetian painter, a small cloth-colourer by trade.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacopo Robusti's nickname comes from his father's trade of dyer (tintore); the -etto ending means little.
explanation.definitionFit: Robusti was the Venetian painter nicknamed for his father's trade, the Italian name meaning small dyer.
